( in Navigation) is an Instrument consisting of two Parts, which are two Circles either, laid one upon, or let into the other, and so fastened, together in their Centers, that they represent two Compasses, one six'd, the other moveable 5 each of them divided into the 32 Points of the Com - fs, and 350 Degrees, and numbred both ways, Both from the North and the South, ending at the East and Weft, in 90 Degrees. The Fixed Comp as represents the Horizon, in which the North, and all the other Points of the Compass are fixed and immoveable. The Moveable Compass represents the Mariners Compass, in which the North, and all the other Points are liable to Variation. In the Centre of the Moveable Compass is fastned a Silk Thread, long enough to reach the out-side of the fixed Compass. But inthe Instrument be made of Wood, there is an Index instead of the Thread. rringinarchitecture.c: RRING, in Architecture, is making good the Rafters-Feet in the Cornish: That is, when Rafters are cut with a Knee, these Furrings, or Furrs, are Pieces that pe straight along with the Rafter from the Top of the Knee to the Cornish. Also when Rafters are rotten, or suck hollow in the Middle, there are Pieces cut thickest in the middle, and tapering towards each End, which are nailed upon them to make them straight; and such Pieces are call'd Furrs, and the putting them on, Furring the Rafters.

In the Foreft of Dean in Gloucefter - ri re, the best Iron Ore is of a bluish Colour, and is called Brufb Ore: But this being melted alone produces a Metal very short and brittle: To remedy which: Inconvenience they make use of Cynder, which is found in great Pi sory where any old Works have been in that County: For in former Times, their Bellows being moved only by Hand, their Furnaces produced a Fire much less intense, than those they now. employ: So that formerly they melted down only the principal Part of the Ore, rejecting the reft as useless. his Refuse is the Cynder; which being mingled with the Ore in a due Quantity, gives it that excellent Temper of Toughness, for which this Iron is preferred before any brought from abroad. The Ore is first calcined in Kilns, like ordinary Lime-Kilns, which they fill up to the Top pad Coal and Ore, S. S. S. " Then putting Fire to the Bottom, they let it burn till the Coal be wafted. This is done without Ffion of the Metal, and serves to consume the more drossy Part of the Ore, and to make it friable. From hence they carry it to the Furnaces, which are buile of Brick or Stone, about 24 Foot qa " ; Ls lor intermix'd with Fuel, which in these Outside, and n ar 30 Foot in Height. Within ri they are not above 8 or 10 Foot over in the middle, and the Top and Bottom have a yet narrower Compass; so they are almost of the Shape of an Egg. Behind the Furnace are placed two very, large Pair of Bellows, whose Nofes meet at a little Hole near the Bottom. These are compressed together by certain Buttons placed on the Axis of a very large Overfbot Wheel. The Furnaces are at first filled with Ore and orks is always of Charcoal, laying them hollow at the Bottom, that they may the more easily take Fire. But after they are once kindled, the Materials run together into a hard Cake or Lump, which is sustain'd by the Fashion of the Furnace 5 and through this the Metal, as it melts, trickles down into the Receivers, where there is a Passage. open, by which they clear away the Scum and Dross. Before thisliesa great Bed of Sand, wherein they make Furrows of what Fashion they please, into which they let their Metal; which is made so very fluent by the Violence of the Fire, that it continues boiling for a good while. The Furnaces are kept at work Day and Night for many Months, still supplying the Waste of the Fuel and other Materials with fresh, pour'd in at the Top. From these Furnaces they bring their Sows and Pigs of Irons ( as they call them) to their Forges. These Forges are of two forts, tho " standing together under the same Roof: And one they call Finery, the other their Chafery. Both of them are ea Heaths, on which they place great Heaps of Sea-Coal, and behind them Bellows, like the former, but not near so large. Into their Finery they first put the Pigs of Iron, placing three or four of them together behind the Fire, with a little of one End thrust into it; where foftning by Degrees, they stir and work them with long Bars of Iron, till the Metal runs together into a round Mass or Lump, which they call an Half Bloom: This they take out, and giving it a few Strokes with their Seats they carry it to great weighty Hammer, raised by the Motion of a Water-Wheel; where applying it dextrously to the Blows, they presently beat it out into a thick short Square: his they put into the Finery again; and heating itred hot, they work it out under the same Hammer, till it comes to be in the Shape of a Bar in the middle, but with two square Knobs on the Ends. Lat of all, they give it other Heats in the Chafery, and more Workings under the Hammer, till they have brought their Irow into Bars of several Shapes and Sizes. If they omit any one Process, it will be sure to want something of its Tough ne / s, which they esteem its Perfection. For the Backs of Chimrieys, Hearths of Ovens, or the like, they take the melted Metal out of the Receivers in great Ladles, and pour it into Moulds of fine Sand. Philof. Trans, N 137. At Miltborpe in Lancafbire they have several Sorts of Iron-Stone, some of it making Coldjbire - Iron; that is, such as is brittle when it is cold. Another fort makes Redjbire, which is such as is apt to break if it be hammer'd when'tis of a dark red Heat; and therefore they are never melted down but in Mixture, and so they yield an indifferent good sort of Iron, They have of late made it much better than before, by melting the Sow - Metal over again, as likewise by using Turf and Charcoal; whereas formerly the Fuel was only Charcoal.. every seventeen Ba er it run.., Tk Oj They first. burn the Iron-Stone, and then for sets of this burnt Stone they put in one of Lime-Stone, unburnt, to. make it melt freely and cast the Cynder, which they al - Ways take off from the melted Iron, before they The Bottom of the Furnace is about two Yards square, and so rises perpendicularly for a Yard or more, which is alf lined within with a Wall of the best Fire-stone, to keep off the Force. of the Fire from the Walls of the Furnace. The Bellows, which are very large, and moved by Water, enter about the middle of the Focus: The reft of the Furnace is raised above this fix or seven Yards / quare-wife, but tapering; so that the top Hole, where they throw in the Mine and Fuel, is but halse Yard quare. When they find ir to have subside about a Yard and Quarter, they sll the Furnace again, Their Forge is much like that of a common Blacksmith's, about one Yard and half over, and of the same Height. The Hearth is all of Sow - Tron, much of the Shape of a Broad - brim'd Hat, with the Crown downwards. The hollow Place they fill and heap up with Charcoal, and lay the Ore ( first broken into Pieces as big asa Pigeon's Egg) all round about the Charcoal on the flat Hearth, to bake it as it were, or neal it; thrusting it by little and little into the Hollow, and keep blowing for twelve Hours. Then they pull out corte at the Bottom of the Wall, and out comes all the GlafJy Cynder, being very liquid, leaving the Iron, which is never in a perfect Fusion, ina Lump at the Bottom: This they take out with great Tongs, and turn it under heavy, Hammers moved by Water, which at. the same time beat off, or rather squeeze out the fluid Scorie or Dross, and after several Heats form it into Bars. They use no Lime-Stone, or any thing else, to promote the Flux. They get about 100 Pound Weight of Metal at one Melting, out of about three times as much Ore.; The Iron Mine in Suffer lies from four Foot deep to forty and upwards. There are several forts of Mine, some hard, some gentle, some rich, some poor, some fine, some courser. The Iron Masters mix different forts of Mine together,. otherwise it will not melt to so good an Advantage. When the Mine is brought in, they take Small - coal, and lay a Row of that and a Row of Mine alternately, S. S. S. one above another; and setting the Coals on Fire, therewith burn the Ore. This is done to mollify it, that so it may be broken in mall Pieces, otherwise it. would not melt in the Furnace, but come away whole: Nor must it be over-burnt; for then it will / oop, as they call it, that is, run together in a Mass, ser tis burnt, tis beat into small Pieces with an Iron Se dee, and then put into the Furnace, which is before charged with Coals, on the Top of which it is cast, where it melts and falls down into the Hearth in about twelve Hours more or less, and then tis run into a Sow. This Hearth is made of Sand-Stone, as also its Sides round to the Height of about a Yard; and then the reft of the Furnace is lined up to the Top with Brick. When they begin upon a new Furnace, they put Fire for a Day or two before they begin to blow: Then they blow gently, and increase by Degrees, till they come to the Height in ten Weeks or more. Every IR O ee ee Every fix Days they call a Fovmday, in which so, that it cot be each into a solid Piece. tine they make 8 Ton of Ivon; that is, if you divide the whote Sum of Iron they make by Poimnday 5 at last more. The Hearth, by the Force of the Fire continasl - ly blown, grows wider and wider so that if at dog man See ee 600 or 700 Pour i at it will contain so sab ch as will oe a Sow of 20 0 Pound. To every Load of Coals ich consists of eleven Quarters, they put a Load of Mine, containing eighteen Bufhels. A Hearth, if made of good Stone, will ordinarily last forty Four days or Weeks; during which time the Fire is never let go out. " They never blow twice on one Hearth, tho they go upon it but five or fix Found ays. The Cynder, Tike Scum, swims upon the melted Metal in the Pree and is let out once or twice before a Sow is cast. In every Forge there are two Fires at least, which, as before By medics are called, one the Finery, and the other the ry.: rs the Finery, by the were ofthe Hammer, they bring it into Blooms and Anconies, thus: They roll the Sow at first into the Fire, dnd then melt off a Piece of about of a hundred Pound Weight; which, as soon as tis broken off, they call a Loop. This Loop they take out with their Shingling-Tongs, and beat it with Iron Sledges on an Bee Plate near the Fire, that so it may not fall in Pieces, but be ina Capacity to be carried under the Hammer; where it is beat gently at first, only to draw Cynders and Dross out of the Matter: But afterwards they let out or draw more Water, and so by degrees beat it thicker and bat till they bring ir to a Bloom; which is a four-quare Mass, about two Foot long. This Operation they call Shingling rhe Loop, This done, they iminediately return it to the Finery again; and after two or three Heats, and Working, they bring it to an Ancony, whose Figure is in the middle a Bar of about three Foot long, and of the Shape they intend the whole Bar shail be made of 5 Bar at both Ends is a quare Piece left ro tigh, to be wrought at the Chafery. At the Chafery they only draw out the two Ends suitable to what was drawn out at the Finery in the middle, and so finish the Bar. reaction.c: REACTION; The Naturalists fay, that Re - striking one against another are exactly equal, but made. with contrary Directions. Or yet in other words by the Action and Reaction of Bo - dies one on another, there are produced equal Changes in each; and those Changes are impressed cowards ( dire tly) contrary Parts, or ways. This will be best understood by Instances: For, whatever Body presses or draws another, is equally pressed or drawn by it again, If any one prefs a Stone with his Finger, his Finger is as much pressed by the Stone: If a Horse by a Rope, Ge. draw a Stone, the Horse shall equally be drawn by the Stone; for the Rope being stretch d both ways, endeavours to relax it self again, and by that means will draw the Horse towards the Stone 5 and will as much hinder the Progression of the Horse, as it forwards the Procession of the Stone. If any Body lighting against another doth by its force any way change its Motion; it self will undergo the same Change in its own proper Motion, but towards contrary Parts, from the Reaction of that Body, and the Equality of irs mutual Pression. By these Actions are produced equal Changes, not indeed of the Velocities, but of the Motions of Bodies; ( ie. in such Bodies as have no Impediment any other way) for the Changes of their Velocities, being made towards contrary Parts, ( because the Motions are equally changed) reciprocally proportional to the Bodies themselves. 5

roundsinagarrison.c: ROUNDS, in a Garrison, is a Night-Watch commanded by an Officer that goes round the Rampart of the Garrison, in order to listen if any thing be stirring without the Works, to fee that the Centres are watchful, and upon Duty, and that all things be in good Order.. In stri & Garrifons, the Rounds go every quarter of an Hour, that the Rampart may be till furnished. The Centres ought to challenge at a Distance; and to test their Arms as the Rounds pas 3, and to let no onecomenearthem. WhentheRowndis near the Corpsdegarde, theCentry calls aloud, Who comes there? And when the Answer is The Rowndshe says, Stand; and then calls for the Corporal of the Guard, who draws his, Sword, and calls also, Who comes there? And when tis answered, The Rouads; he that hath the Word must advance, and deliver the Word to the corporal who receives it with hisSwordpointedat the Giver's Breast.
